question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, because Evans' Generality Constraint requires that grasp of Fa already equips one with the capacity to entertain the open predicate-application Fx for any object-term one possesses; given independent mastery of the universal quantifier, this directly yields the ability to form and understand ∀x Fx as a recombination of those same constituents.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint one should be able to understand ∀x Fx. The constraint requires that grasp of a predicate F in the context of any particular singular term a already involves the capacity to apply that same predicate to any other object in the domain; once universal quantification is separately understood, the open sentence Fx is simply the recombinatory vehicle that lets this capacity be exercised over the whole domain at once. Thus Fa plus quantifier competence yields ∀x Fx without further conceptual resources.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint (GC), understanding Fa (plus universal quantification) entails the ability to understand ∀x Fx. GC requires that possession of the concept F enables its free recombination with any singular term one can grasp, yielding Fb, Fc, etc. Given independent grasp of ∀, these instances can be collected under a single quantified thought ranging over the relevant domain, so ∀x Fx follows directly from the recombinatorial structure GC imposes on conceptual thought.

(The constraint is silent on whether one must also grasp higher-order or non-objectual predication, but that is outside the question's scope.)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint (GC), grasp of Fa already equips one with a fully recombinable, general concept F. Given independent mastery of the universal quantifier, this immediately licenses grasp of ∀x Fx, since GC demands that F be applicable to every object in the domain one can think about. GC does not merely permit isolated singular instances; it enforces systematic generality across both singular and quantified contexts. 

(The GC is silent on how one acquires quantificational concepts themselves, but the question stipulates that this is already in place.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, understanding Fa does not entail the ability to understand ∀x Fx merely by the Generality Constraint (plus grasp of the quantifier). GC requires only that the thinker can recombine the grasped predicate F with any other object of which they can think (e.g., Fb, Fc …), thereby ensuring that F functions as a general concept. It does not require the further capacity to collect every object in the domain under a single universally quantified thought; that step needs independent resources about the domain’s extent and the quantifier’s semantics, which GC itself does not supply.

(The question’s phrasing “Fx (∀x)” is read as the closed sentence ∀x Fx; if it were instead the open matrix Fx, GC would of course already guarantee its intelligibility once F and the relevant variable are grasped.)

GC demands that possession of the singular thought Fa rests on a general, recombinable grasp of the constituent concepts: the same thinker who understands Fa must be able to substitute any other object of thought for a while keeping F fixed. This recombinability already shows that F is not tied idiosyncratically to a; it is a genuinely general predicate. Once the thinker also possesses the quantifier concept ∀x, nothing further is needed to apply that predicate to the entire domain, yielding ∀x Fx. Thus GC plus quantifier competence directly licenses the universally quantified thought.

(The converse does not hold: one could master ∀x Fx without yet having singular thoughts about particular objects, but the question only concerns the direction Fa → ∀x Fx.)

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint, grasping Fa should allow one to grasp ∀x Fx once universal quantification is already understood. 14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint, grasping Fa already equips one to understand ∀x Fx once universal quantification is mastered. Universal quantification simply generalizes that same capacity over the domain, so the transition from Fa to ∀x Fx is licensed by the recombinability the constraint demands. Any apparent gap would imply that F is not fully general after all, violating the constraint.

Even when the quantifier notation itself is understood, forming ∀x Fx demands an additional layer of generality not entailed by singular-thought recombinability alone.

(The constraint is therefore compatible with someone who can entertain every instance Fa, Fb, … they can formulate yet still lack a unified, domain-wide universal thought.)

The constraint is precisely what ensures that possession of the atomic thought already equips the thinker to project F universally rather than only to the particular object a.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building on the points from colleagues 12 and 14, the Generality Constraint already supplies the open predicate abstraction needed once we have Fa: grasp of F is not tethered to a but is available for systematic recombination with any understood device, including the bound variable x whose quantificational binding we have separately mastered. If the constraint did not already underwrite that projection across the domain, it would be hard to see how F counts as a genuine concept at all.

2.text:
No. Evans' Generality Constraint (GC) is formulated strictly in terms of singular recombinability: grasp of Fa requires the capacity to entertain Fb (etc.) for any other object b of which one already has a conception, thereby ensuring F functions as a genuinely general predicate rather than an idiosyncratic attachment to a. This does not by itself underwrite the further move to a single, domain-wide thought ∀x Fx. Even when the quantifier is independently mastered, GC supplies no resources for collecting the (potentially open-ended or infinite) totality of objects under one bound variable; that step requires additional apparatus concerning the semantics of quantification and the extent of the domain. Hence the constraint is compatible with a thinker who can form every singular instance yet still lack the unified quantified thought.

(The question's phrasing “Fx (∀x)” is interpreted as the closed sentence ∀x Fx; if it were the open matrix alone, GC would of course already guarantee its intelligibility.)
